# Step

```{r}
#| include: false
source("../R/setup.R")
```

How do you draw a value that holds until it jumps? `step` draws it as a
staircase. A `line` slopes straight from one point to the next. A `step`
**holds** each value until it changes, then jumps. The **flat part** runs from
one observation to the next, and the **jump** is where the value changes. That
is the right shape for anything that does not change between observations: a
cumulative count, a survival probability, an interest rate. `step` takes the
same channels as `line`, and only the path drawn between two points differs.

Several professions draw this shape, each under its own name, and `step` draws
each of these plots from a table that holds its values. Statisticians draw the **empirical cumulative distribution
function** (the empirical CDF) with it. Medical researchers draw the **survival
curve**, the Kaplan–Meier estimate [@kaplan1958], which drops at each observed
death. Reliability engineers draw the same staircase for parts rather than
patients, and call it a failure plot. Analysts in finance draw the **step
chart** of a rate that holds until someone changes it. A cumulative count rises
and a survival probability falls, and `step` draws both as this one staircase.

## A step function {#a-step-function}

What share of European countries have a life expectancy at or below 75 years,
or 80, or any value you choose? The empirical CDF answers all of those questions
at once. It is a **step function**: flat between observations, with a jump at
each one. The `gm_europe_cdf` table holds one row for each of the 30 European
countries in 2007: its life expectancy, and the share of countries at or below
it. Each country's share is its rank by life expectancy divided by 30: the
lowest has 1/30, about 0.033, and the highest has 1. The table already holds
the shares, so `step` needs no transform: give it an `x` and a `y`, and it
draws the curve:

```{r}
#| echo: false
peek(gm_europe_cdf)
```

```{r}
data(gm_europe_cdf) + step + x(life) + y(share) +
  x_label("Life expectancy (years)") + y_label("Cumulative share of countries") +
  title("Empirical CDF of life expectancy in Europe, 2007")
```

*"Given the gm europe cdf table: a step outline, x is life, y is share."*

At 75 years the curve is at about 0.27, so 8 of the 30 countries have a life
expectancy of 75 years or less. At 80 it is at about 0.77, so 23 do. A `line` on this same
table would slope between points, so between two countries it would show
shares such as 1.5/30, which no number of countries can make. The step is
exact: between two countries no country is added, so the share does not
change.

The [`cumulative` transform](../transforms.qmd#cumulative-the-running-total)
computes the same shares from the countries themselves. On a continuous axis,
`count` tallies the rows at each distinct value, and `cumulative(share = TRUE)`
adds the tallies up and divides each running total by the 30 rows, so the curve
ends at 1. The `gm_europe` table holds the same 30
countries, with no share column:

```{r}
#| echo: false
peek(gm_europe)
```

```{r}
data(gm_europe) + step * count * cumulative(share = TRUE) + x(life) +
  x_label("Life expectancy (years)") + y_label("Cumulative share of countries") +
  title("The same curve, computed by cumulative")
```

*"Given gapminder Europe: a step outline derived by count and cumulative as
shares, x is life."*

The curve is the same as the one above. It starts at 1/30 at the lowest
country, Turkey, and rises at each of the other 29. With `bin` in place of
`count`, it rises once for each bin that holds a country instead.

Whether you can see the flat parts depends on how many observations there are.
With thirty countries, each jump is 1/30 of the height from 0 to 1, and most of
the flat parts between them are easy to see. The `gapminder_2007` table holds
one row for each of 142 countries in 2007. Over all of them, each jump is about
a fifth as tall as here, and the staircase reads as a slightly rough line:

```{r}
#| echo: false
peek(gapminder_2007)
```

```{r}
data(gapminder_2007) + step * count * cumulative(share = TRUE) + x(life) +
  x_label("Life expectancy (years)") + y_label("Cumulative share of countries") +
  title("The same curve over 142 countries")
```

## A value that holds until it changes {#a-value-that-holds-until-it-changes}

A step is also the right mark for anything that jumps rather than changing
gradually: a policy rate (the interest rate a central bank sets), a price, an
inventory level. Each holds its value, then jumps on a single day. A straight
line would draw a gradual change that never happened. The `policy_rates` table
holds one interest rate for each year from 2018 to 2023, and a step draws it:

```{r}
#| echo: false
peek(policy_rates)
```

```{r}
data(policy_rates) + step + x(year) + y(rate) +
  x_label("Year") + y_label("Policy rate (%)") +
  title("A rate rises, falls, holds two years, then rises twice")
```

The rate fell to 0.25 in 2020 and held there for two full years, then rose
twice. A line would have sloped into and out of that flat part, showing rates
that were never set.

## Multiple series {#multiple-series}

The policy rate was a single **series**, one set of rows drawn as one
staircase, and often you need to compare two. The `inventory` table holds the
units in stock at two sites, North and South, for each of eight weeks. Only a
delivery or a sale changes a site's stock. To compare the sites week by week,
you want both on one plot. `color` and `group` split a `step` exactly as they
split a `line`: one staircase per category. `color` also gives each staircase
its own color and a legend entry; `group` splits without either. Here two series
hold and jump independently:

```{r}
#| echo: false
peek(inventory)
```

```{r}
data(inventory) + step + x(week) + y(units) + color(site) +
  x_label("Week") + y_label("Units in stock") +
  title("Inventory by site: each site holds until it changes")
```

*"Given the inventory: step outlines, x is week, y is units, color by site."*

North holds at 40 for two weeks, then falls twice before jumping to 55. South
starts lower, rises above North in week 5, and falls below it again in week 7.
Neither series slopes between its changes.

## A category on the domain {#a-category-on-the-domain}

Every `x` so far has been a number. How does the mean life expectancy compare
across continents? A step will draw that plot, but a bar is the better mark for it,
as the step drawn below shows. A step reads one axis as its **domain**, the
axis it runs along, and the other as its **measure**, the quantity it traces.
A category is always the domain, so here the domain is `x`. A category on the
domain gets one slot per value, an equal stretch of the axis for each
continent, as in [Line](line.qmd#a-category-on-the-domain-the-profile). The staircase holds each
continent's mean from the center of its slot to the center of the next one:

```{r}
data(gapminder_2007) + step * mean + x(continent) + y(life) +
  y_label("Mean life expectancy") +
  title("step * mean + x(continent): the five means as a staircase")
```

*"Given gapminder 2007: a step outline derived by mean, x is continent, y is
life."*

Africa is lowest at 54.8 years and Oceania highest at 80.7. Oceania, the last
slot, has no next slot, so its mean is only the top of the last jump. The five
slots run in the order the continents first appear in the table. That order
means nothing, so the rise and fall across the slots is not a trend.

Every flat part of a step is at one of the five means. A `line` slopes from
one category to the next, so between them it passes through heights that are no
continent's mean.

That does not make it the right mark for this plot. A flat part claims that the
value held across the part of the axis under it. A policy rate does hold
between two dates, as [A value that holds until it
changes](#a-value-that-holds-until-it-changes) showed. Between two continents
there is no value to hold, so the flat part there says nothing about the data.
One summary value per category is what a [bar](bar.qmd) draws: keep the `mean`
and change the mark. Each bar is in its own slot, joined to nothing.

Other marks take the same `mean`, and only the shape changes:

| Mark derived by `mean` | Shape |
|---|---|
| `bar * mean` | one bar per category, each in its own slot |
| `point * mean` | one dot at each mean |
| `line * mean` | the means joined into a profile |
| `area * mean` | the same profile, filled to the baseline |
| `step * mean` | each mean held flat until the next category, the plot above |

gog draws this step and prints no warning. It never refuses a sentence only
because another mark would show the data better, so the choice of mark is yours
([Law 8](../design-laws.qmd#law-8-pronounceable-usable)).

A staircase can also turn, as [the line's profile](line.qmd#the-profile-turned)
does, which gives long category names room down the left side. With the
continents on `y`, the staircase is read down the page:

```{r}
data(gapminder_2007) + step * mean + x(life) + y(continent) +
  x_label("Mean life expectancy") +
  title("step * mean + y(continent): the staircase, turned")
```

Each mean is now held from its slot down to the next one, so the parts that
hold a mean are vertical and the jumps are horizontal. Oceania, the last slot,
again has no next slot, so its mean is only the end of the last jump.

## Histogram outline {#histogram-outline}

`mean` is not the only transform a step takes. With `bin`, the staircase
answers a question that filled bars make harder to read: how do three
distributions compare in one panel? The `iris_flowers` table holds measurements
of 150 iris flowers, 50 of each of three species. Filled histograms of the three
overlap wherever two species share a bin, as the Bar chapter's [Overlaid
histograms](bar.qmd#overlaid-histograms) section shows. gog fades those fills so the shapes underneath still show,
but the faded colors mix where they overlap. A step has no fill at all, so
nothing needs fading. `step * bin` draws a histogram as an **outline** rather
than as bars: one staircase along the tops of the bins. Add `color` and the
outline splits, one staircase per group, cut on the same bins:

```{r}
#| echo: false
peek(iris_flowers)
```

```{r}
data(iris_flowers) + step * bin + x(petal_length) + color(species) +
  x_label("Petal length (cm)") + title("Petal length by species: step outline")
```

*"Given the iris flowers: step outlines derived by bin, x is petal length, color
by species."*

`bin` cuts all three species into the same bins, so their outlines share the
same edges. An outline goes to zero in any bin where its species has no rows.

The same `bin` works with other marks, and only the mark changes:

| Mark derived by `bin` | Shape |
|---|---|
| `bar * bin` | filled bars |
| `line * bin` | frequency polygon: one stroke of straight pieces through the bin centers |
| `area * bin` | the same polygon, filled to the baseline |
| `step * bin` | the staircase outline above |

## Stroke width and opacity {#stroke-width-and-opacity}

The three outlines above are thin, and where two of them run along the same bin
edge, the one drawn last covers the other. A thicker stroke is easier to see,
and a little transparency lets the covered stroke show through. Like `line`, a
`step` is a
single stroke per series, so on a step `size` and `opacity` cannot be mapped to
a column; they are settings for the whole stroke:

```{r}
data(iris_flowers) + step * bin + x(petal_length) + color(species) +
  style(size = 2.5, opacity = 0.7) +
  x_label("Petal length (cm)") + title("A thicker, more transparent outline")
```

*"Given the iris flowers: step outlines derived by bin, x is petal length, color
by species, with size 2.5 and opacity 0.7."*

`size` sets the stroke width. `opacity` makes the whole staircase more
transparent. Both are set, never mapped, exactly as on a `line`;
[Setting vs mapping](../style.qmd) explains the difference.

## Transforms it takes {#transforms-it-takes}

A transform computes new values from the rows, and the mark draws those values
instead of the rows. The table lists, by kind, the transforms a step takes and
the ones it refuses:

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| results: asis
mark_transforms("step")
```

The plots below show every transform a step takes. Within a figure the plots
differ mainly in their transform, and the paragraph before each figure names any
other change.

**Counting.** `count` and `proportion` tally the rows at each value of `x`, on a
category or a number. `bin` and `density` work on a number. `bin` counts the
rows in each interval, and `density` estimates, as a smooth curve, how closely
the rows lie along the axis. Each puts its result on the axis you leave empty.
The top two plots put `continent` on `x`, and the bottom two put `life`. With
`continent` on `x`, the staircase holds each count from the center of one slot
to the center of the next. [A category on the domain](#a-category-on-the-domain)
draws the same shape with `mean`. `step * bin` draws the same kind of outline as
[Histogram outline](#histogram-outline). `step * density` draws the density
curve as many small steps:

```{r}
((data(gapminder_2007) + step * count + x(continent) + title("step * count")) |
  (data(gapminder_2007) + step * proportion + x(continent) +
     title("step * proportion"))) /
  ((data(gapminder_2007) + step * bin + x(life) + title("step * bin")) |
     (data(gapminder_2007) + step * density + x(life) + title("step * density")))
```

*"Given gapminder 2007: a step outline derived by count, x is continent, beside
a step outline derived by proportion, x is continent; above a step outline
derived by bin, x is life, beside a step outline derived by density, x is
life."*

The axis you leave empty is `y`, so look at it in each plot. All four sentences
leave out `y()`, yet each `y` axis has a name: Count, Proportion, Count and
Density. The table has no column by those names. Each transform writes one, and
`y` draws it. `count` and `bin` write `count`, the number of rows at each value
or in each interval. `proportion` writes `proportion`, each count's share of all
the rows. `density` writes `density`, the height of the estimated curve. The
axis is labeled with the column's name, capitalized, as [The name on a measure
axis](../transforms.qmd#the-name-on-a-measure-axis) explains.

The two plots on top have the same shape, because each proportion is a count
divided by 142, the number of countries.

**Summaries.** The six summaries reduce the rows at each value of `x` to one
value, so they need a number on `y`. The `gm_all` table holds 142
countries, measured every five years from 1952 to 2007, so each year has 142
rows:

```{r}
#| echo: false
peek(gm_all)
```

`sum` reads `population`, because only an amount has a total that means
something. The other five read `life`. They give the mean, the median, the
largest and the smallest value, and `quantile(0.9)` gives the value that nine
tenths of the rows fall below. Each staircase holds a year's value until the
next measurement, five years later:

```{r}
((data(gm_all) + step * sum + x(year) + y(population) +
    title("step * sum")) |
  (data(gm_all) + step * mean + x(year) + y(life) +
     title("step * mean")) |
  (data(gm_all) + step * median + x(year) + y(life) +
     title("step * median"))) /
  ((data(gm_all) + step * max + x(year) + y(life) +
      title("step * max")) |
     (data(gm_all) + step * min + x(year) + y(life) +
        title("step * min")) |
     (data(gm_all) + step * quantile(0.9) + x(year) + y(life) +
        title("step * quantile(0.9)")))
```

*"Given all the gapminder years: a step outline derived by sum, x is year, y is
population, beside a step outline derived by mean, x is year, y is life, beside
a step outline derived by median, x is year, y is life; above a step outline
derived by max, x is year, y is life, beside a step outline derived by min, x is
year, y is life, beside a step outline derived by quantile at 0.9, x is year, y
is life."*

The five plots that read `life` share one scale, so their heights can be
compared from plot to plot. Only `min` falls as well as rises. It falls twice:
from 35.4 years in 1972 to Cambodia's 31.2 in 1977, and from 39.9 years in 1987
to Rwanda's 23.6 in 1992.

**Fitted lines.** `smooth` and `straight` need a number on each axis. They fit a
line to the rows, each placed at its `x` and its `y`. `smooth` follows the
shape of the data, and `straight` is the least-squares line. A step draws each
fitted line as a staircase of very small steps, one at each of the evenly spaced
places along `x`: 100 unless you set `places`.

**Running total.** `cumulative` adds each value to the ones before it along the
axis. The third plot reads the `quarterly` table, with `year` on `x` and `sales`
on `y`. The table, despite its name, holds one year of sales in each row. A
running total changes only when a year's sales are added, so a staircase suits
it:

```{r}
#| echo: false
peek(quarterly)
```

```{r}
((data(gapminder_2007) + step * smooth + x(gdp) + y(life) +
    title("step * smooth")) |
   (data(gapminder_2007) + step * straight + x(gdp) + y(life) +
      title("step * straight")) |
   (data(quarterly) + step * cumulative + x(year) + y(sales) +
      title("step * cumulative"))) +
  theme(height = 450)
```

*"Given gapminder 2007: a step outline derived by smooth, x is gdp, y is life,
beside a step outline derived by straight, x is gdp, y is life; beside a step
outline from quarterly, derived by cumulative, x is year, y is sales."*

**Pairs.** The pair transforms give `y` a low and a high at each value of `x`,
and a step draws each of the two as its own staircase. `range`, `confidence` and
`deviation` read a number on `y`, and like the summaries they reduce the rows at
each value of `x`. `range` gives the smallest and the largest value.
`confidence` gives the 95% confidence interval of the mean, and `deviation`
reaches one standard deviation from the mean on each side. Both also compute the
mean itself, which a step leaves out:

```{r}
((data(gm_all) + step * range + x(year) + y(life) + title("step * range")) |
   (data(gm_all) + step * confidence + x(year) + y(life) +
      title("step * confidence")) |
   (data(gm_all) + step * deviation + x(year) + y(life) +
      title("step * deviation"))) +
  theme(height = 450)
```

*"Given all the gapminder years: a step outline derived by range, x is year, y
is life, beside a step outline derived by confidence, x is year, y is life,
beside a step outline derived by deviation, x is year, y is life."*

The two staircases of `confidence` differ by about 4 years of life expectancy in
every year, because the mean of 142 values varies little. The two staircases of
`deviation` differ by 21 to 25 years, because they show how far the countries
spread.

The other three pairs do not reduce the rows at each value of `x`.
`smooth_band` and `straight_band` fit the same line as `smooth` and `straight`,
and give a low and a high around it at the same evenly spaced places along `x`.
Like those two, they
need a number on each axis. `bounds` computes nothing: it reads the low and the
high from two columns you name, and it needs no `y`. The third plot reads the
`score_band` table, with `score` on `x`. The table holds a low and a high for
each raw score on a test scored from 0 to 20. The analysis computed them before
the plot, and gog only draws them:

```{r}
#| echo: false
peek(score_band)
```

```{r}
((data(gapminder_2007) + step * smooth_band + x(gdp) + y(life) +
    title("step * smooth_band")) |
   (data(gapminder_2007) + step * straight_band + x(gdp) + y(life) +
      title("step * straight_band")) |
   (data(score_band) + step * bounds(lower, upper) + x(score) +
      title("step * bounds"))) +
  theme(height = 450)
```

*"Given gapminder 2007: a step outline derived by smooth_band, x is gdp, y is
life, beside a step outline derived by straight_band, x is gdp, y is life;
beside a step outline from the score band, from lower to upper, x is score."*

A step refuses every transform in the Refuses column above. These are the same
transforms a [`line`](line.qmd) refuses. The collision modifiers move marks that
would be drawn on top of one another, such as [`bar`](bar.qmd) and
[`point`](point.qmd). A step is a thin stroke, so two staircases that meet cross
instead. To pile one series on another, use `stack` with [`area`](area.qmd).
`repel` moves only [`text`](text.qmd) labels. `partition`, `flow` and `cluster`
lay out rectangles, bands and branches, which [`zone`](zone.qmd),
[`ribbon`](ribbon.qmd) and [`path`](path.qmd) draw. `layout` places a network,
which [`point`](point.qmd), [`text`](text.qmd) and [`edge`](edge.qmd) draw.

## What you can set {#what-you-can-set}

A setting changes how the staircase looks without reading a column, and each
mark takes its own. [Setting vs mapping](../style.qmd) shows how a setting differs from mapping a
column. These are a step's settings, with the values each accepts:

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| results: asis
mark_options("step")
```

A step is a stroke, so it takes exactly what `line` takes: one color, one width,
one opacity and one dash for the whole staircase. Mapped to a column instead of
set, `color` alone can change *along* the staircase, as the last plot in
[What it refuses](#what-it-refuses) shows.

Set three of them at once and the staircase changes color, width and dash
together. The `six_weeks` table holds 42 consecutive days of `orders`. Its `day`
column holds dates, so the x axis is a calendar axis. A CSV file cannot record that
a column holds dates, so after reading the table, with `gog_table()` or any other
reader, convert the column; [A date](../book-data.qmd#a-date) shows how:

```{r}
#| echo: false
peek(six_weeks)
```

```{r}
data(six_weeks) + step + x(day) + y(orders) +
  style(color = "purple", size = 2.5, pattern = "dotted") +
  y_label("Orders") + title("A dotted staircase")
```

*"Given the six weeks table: a step outline, x is day, y is orders, colored
purple, with size 2.5 and pattern dotted."*

The staircase and the dash change different things. The staircase decides
where the path goes: it puts a corner wherever the value changes. The dash
decides only how the path looks, never where it goes. That is why `step` is a
mark, while a dash only changes how a mark is drawn.

The [grid of every mark and every setting](../style.qmd#what-you-can-set) shows
which other marks share this list. What a mark *maps* rather than sets is its
row on the [grid of marks and channels](../combinations.qmd#marks-and-channels).

## What it refuses {#what-it-refuses}

A step refuses four kinds of sentence: a mapped `size` or `opacity`, a hatch
pattern, a category on both axes, and a split that leaves one position in every
series. A step is one connected stroke with no filled interior, and the first
two refusals follow from that. The third comes from the value a step traces,
and the fourth from a series that holds a single position.

One stroke has one width, the same at every place along it. So no column can
make the staircase wider in one place than in another. The `gapminder_asia`
table holds five Asian countries, measured every five years from 1952 to 2007:

```{r}
#| echo: false
peek(gapminder_asia)
```

```{r}
#| error: true
data(gapminder_asia) + step + x(year) + y(life) + size(gdp)
```

The stroke still *has* a width, and `style(size = )` sets it. `size(column)`
asks for a width per row, which one stroke cannot give. A mapped `opacity` is
refused for the same reason: the stroke has one opacity. That distinction is the
subject of [Setting vs mapping](../style.qmd).

The second refusal is about which patterns a stroke accepts. A hatch is a
texture that fills an area, and a staircase is a stroke with no area to fill:

```{r}
#| error: true
data(gapminder_asia) + step + x(year) + y(life) + style(pattern = "hatch")
```

The third refusal is one that `line`, `area` and `ribbon * range` give too. A step
traces a value across categories, and with a category on both axes there is no
value to trace:

```{r}
#| error: true
data(gapminder_2007) + step + x(continent) + y(country)
```

The fourth is shared by `line`, `area`, `ribbon` and `path`. A staircase needs at
least two positions in each series. A plot in which every series holds one would draw
nothing, so gog refuses it, as [Line](line.qmd#what-it-refuses) shows.

A `color` mapped to a column is not refused: it is the one property that can change along a single
staircase. This is the plot promised in [What you can set](#what-you-can-set).
A width and a dash belong to the whole stroke. A dash can still change from one
series to the next, as it does for a `line`, but never along one series. A
color belongs to each place on the stroke instead, so a column can change it
from one row to the next. Each flat part takes its row's color, and each jump
blends the colors of the two rows it joins:

```{r}
data(gapminder_asia) + step + x(year) + y(life) + group(country) +
  color(gdp, scale = "log") + palette("viridis") +
  y_label("Life expectancy") + title("Each country's staircase, colored by its income")
```

*"Given gapminder Asia: step outlines, x is year, y is life, grouped by country,
color by gdp on a log scale, with the viridis palette."*

`scale = "log"` makes equal ratios of income equal steps of color: each tenfold
rise in income moves the color by the same amount. `palette()` chooses the colors a mapping uses.
`"viridis"` is a [ramp](../channels.qmd#ramps), and the named palettes and what
each is for are in [Palettes](../channels.qmd#palettes).

Read one country's staircase from left to right and you see two variables. The
height is how long people live, and the color is how rich the country was then.
The color stays the same along each flat part and changes only at the jumps,
where the value changes too.

## In short {#in-short}

A step holds each value until it changes, so between two observations it
draws no value that was not in the data. It takes the same channels and
settings as a `line`: width and opacity belong to the whole stroke, and only
`color` varies along it. With `color`, `group` or a mapped `pattern` it draws
one staircase per category, and with `bin` it draws
a histogram as an outline instead of as bars.

## What comes next {#what-comes-next}

Each staircase has one value at each `x`. [Interval](interval.qmd) spans
two values at every position instead, from a low one to a high one.
